claims.text: The test alloy is initially a uniform, single-phase, equiatomic or near-equiatomic multi-principal-element solid solution.
High strain-rate loading induces localized changes in chemical ordering in an initially single-phase HEA.
Cyclic loading induces localized changes in chemical ordering in an initially single-phase HEA.
High strain-rate or cyclic loading can induce nano-precipitate formation in the initially single-phase alloy.
Loading-induced microstructural evolution is localized near crack tips and within deformation bands.
Breakdown of short-range chemical order during cyclic loading creates locally softer, higher-energy regions and changes stacking-fault behavior.
Severe loading reduces effective barriers for dislocation motion.
Dislocation-mediated deformation mechanisms can act synergistically to produce high toughness in an HEA.
Loading-induced ordering changes or nano-precipitates suppress the synergistic contributions of dislocation glide, twinning, and extrinsic toughening.
Suppression of these toughening mechanisms causes a sudden reduction in fracture toughness.
High strain-rate or cyclic loading promotes a transition to brittle fracture.
Dynamically or cyclically loaded specimens will show detectable microstructural transformations by in situ TEM or SEM.
The dynamically or cyclically loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness than quasi-static specimens.
Quasi-static specimens retain a homogeneous single-phase microstructure under loading.
Quasi-static specimens exhibit ductile behavior through established dislocation-based toughening mechanisms.
High strain-rate or cyclic loading represents demanding engineering service conditions for the proposed alloy.
Elevated service temperature may challenge phase stability and alter the proposed effect.
